newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: NZ's Lange denies predicting Labour defections.
newsitem.headline: NZ's Lange denies predicting Labour defections.

text.p: New Zealand's former Labour Prime Minister David Lange said on Friday he was misreported and had not predicted a rush of defections from Labour to the conservative National Party after the October 12 election.

Questioned in a radio interview about his comments in an Australian television interview, he said he "wasn't advocating it, I certainly wasn't predicting a mass of defections and I certainly wasn't limiting it at all to the Labour Party".
"MMP is about getting people to change positions and the prime minister (Jim Bolger) knows that," Lange said.

He said Bolger "could use his office, if he has enough votes on election night, to coerce, seduce, cajole and wheedle people from other parties...into his government by offering them the perquisites of office."
Referring to other previous defections from Labour and National, Lange said: "All I'm saying is political loyalty seems to have a rather low premium placed on it lately."
Lange's reported TV comments were described by Labour deputy leader Michael Cullen as unhelpful to Labour, which is bidding to lead a coalition government to oust National after the election.

Deputy Prime Minister Don McKinnon challenged Lange to name the MPs he thinks will join National and confirm if "any of these are the same...members who have been quietly signalling to the National Party that they could find some accommodation with National after the election."
New Zealand First leader Winston Peters, Labour's most likely coalition partner, said Lange's comments had betrayed Labour's real problem, "a lack of unity in its ranks," NZPA reported.

Both Lange and Lion Nathan chief executive Doug Myers, who was interviewed on the same Australian television programme, agreed New Zealand would not undergo any change in its economic direction as a result of the election.
Lange said no realistic potential coalition was determined to upset the current policy.

Myers said most New Zealanders wanted a continuation of the current economic direction and New Zealand would continue to prosper, although it seemed that getting complex legislation through parliament would be more difficult.

Lange poured cold water on any possibility that Labour, the Alliance and NZ First would form a coalition after the election. There was too much hatred, ill-will, history and madness, he said. -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473 4746
